V01.answer: Yes — plan to introduce yourself to the banjar (the neighbourhood council) soon after you move in. Canggu's customary village rules treat someone renting here without being a registered member as a tamiu, a guest, and they ask guests to report to the local officials within one wuku — seven days — with clear documents. You should also expect a monthly community contribution; each banjar sets its own amount and way of collecting it, so ask yours directly. Your landlord or host can tell you which banjar your house belongs to and who to speak to.
V01.why_it_matters: Letting the banjar know who is living where is how the community keeps track of its residents and shares the cost of neighbourhood and temple life.
recommended_actions: Report to your local banjar within your first week, bringing clear documents for identification.
Ask your landlord or host which banjar your rented house belongs to.
Ask the banjar about the monthly community contribution and how it is paid.

V01.search_translation: Aku menyewa rumah di Canggu selama dua bulan. Apa aku harus melapor ke banjar?

V02.answer: Ya, menurut aturan adat Desa Adat Canggu, pendatang seperti Anda memang diminta melapor. Dalam satu wuku (tujuh hari) sejak tinggal di sini, laporkan diri ke prajuru dinas (pengurus desa) dengan dokumen yang jelas, lalu bayar sadana krama, yaitu iuran kependudukan, setiap bulan. Kalau Anda beragama Hindu, laporannya juga ke prajuru adat. Besaran iuran dan tata cara pendaftaran ditentukan masing-masing banjar (dewan lingkungan tempat Anda tinggal), jadi sebaiknya tanyakan langsung ke banjar setempat. Ini soal ketertiban dan supaya keberadaan Anda tercatat di lingkungan.
V02.why_it_matters: Melapor membuat kehadiran Anda dikenal oleh banjar dan tetangga, sehingga Anda bisa tinggal dengan tenang dan ikut menjaga kehidupan lingkungan bersama.
recommended_actions: Lapor ke prajuru dinas di kantor desa dalam tujuh hari sejak mulai tinggal di Canggu, bawa dokumen yang jelas.
Tanyakan ke banjar setempat soal sadana krama (iuran kependudukan) dan cara pendaftarannya.
Kalau Anda beragama Hindu, laporkan juga diri Anda ke prajuru adat.
Simpan bukti lapor dan pembayaran iuran untuk jaga-jaga.

V02.search_translation: I'm a visitor who lives in the Incancan. Am I obliged to report to the custom?

V03.answer: Yes—separate your household rubbish at the villa, and keep single-use plastic out of your daily routine. Canggu's customary village rules (awig-awig / pararem) apply to guests staying in households here, so you're asked to manage what you produce: use recyclable or easily compostable packaging, set up five separate containers for sorted waste, and keep the types apart. Sellable inorganic waste goes to the shared waste unit or your banjar's sekaa resik (waste group) on the set schedule; non-sellable inorganic and residual waste is put out for village collection. When you're out, take your rubbish with you or put it in the proper place.
V03.why_it_matters: Keeping waste sorted helps protect shared places like streets, drains and beaches, and it fits the gotong royong spirit of everyone pitching in.
recommended_actions: Set up five separate containers at your villa for sorted household waste.
Avoid single-use plastic and choose recyclable or easily compostable packaging.
Deliver sellable inorganic waste to the shared waste unit or your banjar's sekaa resik on the set schedule.
Put non-sellable inorganic and residual waste out for collection by the village waste unit.

V03.search_translation: Bagaimana aku harus mengurus sampah rumah tanggaku di vilaku di Canggu?

V04.answer: Ya, sampah rumah tangga di Canggu perlu dipilah dan dikelola, termasuk oleh tamiu (tamu atau pendatang, termasuk warga asing yang tinggal sementara). Dalam aturan adat Canggu (pararem), setiap rumah tangga diminta menyediakan lima wadah terpisah sesuai jenis sampah, lalu memilah sampah ke wadah itu. Kurangi plastik sekali pakai dan pilih kemasan yang bisa didaur ulang atau mudah terurai. Sampah anorganik yang masih bernilai jual diserahkan ke unit pengelola sampah bersama atau pengurus kebersihan banjar (sekaa resik) sesuai jadwal; sampah anorganik tanpa nilai jual dan residu diletakkan di tempat yang akan diambil petugas desa.
V04.why_it_matters: Karena kebersihan dan kelestarian lingkungan Canggu adalah tanggung jawab bersama warga dan tamu, bukan hanya soal rumah sendiri.
recommended_actions: Siapkan lima wadah sampah terpisah sesuai jenisnya di rumah.
Pilah sampah rumah tangga ke wadah yang sesuai.
Kurangi plastik sekali pakai dan pilih kemasan yang bisa didaur ulang atau mudah terurai.
Serahkan sampah anorganik bernilai jual ke unit pengelola sampah bersama atau sekaa resik di banjar sesuai jadwal.

V04.search_translation: How do you sort out household garbage in the Incant?

V05.answer: Yes — if you don't sort your rubbish properly, the village waste service can simply stop collecting from you. Canggu's customary village rules (awig-awig / pararem) on waste say that anyone who doesn't sort properly loses the village collection service. For more serious or repeated things — dumping rubbish in drains, rivers, the sea or on roadsides, burning it, or letting it pile up — there's a ladder: a friendly word on the spot, then a formal warning, then a customary fine decided by the village officials. That fine can be the price of 10 to 100 kg of premium rice, a day cleaning public areas, or a purification ceremony.
V05.why_it_matters: Waste here isn't just a tidiness issue — the rules treat pollution as damage to the village itself, including its temples and shared spaces, so sorting at home is part of being a good guest.
recommended_actions: Separate your rubbish before you put it out for collection
Use the proper bins or collection point rather than drains, roadsides or rivers
Never burn rubbish without approval from the village officials
Ask your host or the local banjar (neighbourhood council) how collection and sorting work where you stay

V05.search_translation: Apa yang terjadi jika aku tidak memisahkan sampahku di Canggu? Apakah ada sanksi?

V06.answer: Saat Nyepi, yang tidak boleh dilakukan adalah menyalakan api atau lampu, bekerja, bepergian, dan membuat suara keras atau bersenang-senang. Aturan ini tertulis dalam awig-awig Canggu untuk warga desa adat, jadi sebagai tamu cara terbaik menghormatinya adalah ikut menjaga suasana hening: tetap di akomodasi, tidak keluar ke jalan, dan tidak berpesta. Ada pengecualian kecil untuk bayi di bawah tiga bulan, orang sakit, dan jenazah, tapi itu urusan rumah tangga warga. Sehari setelah Nyepi disebut Ngembak Geni, saat orang saling memaafkan dan aktivitas kembali normal.
V06.why_it_matters: Nyepi adalah hari yoga semadi, dan keheningan seluruh desa itulah bentuk penghormatan bersama yang membuat hari itu terasa sakral bagi orang Bali.
recommended_actions: Tetap di dalam akomodasi sepanjang hari Nyepi dan jangan keluar ke jalan.
Hindari menyalakan api atau lampu terang di luar keperluan penting.
Jangan memutar musik keras atau mengadakan pesta; jaga suasana tetap sunyi.
Tanyakan ke tuan rumah atau pengelola akomodasi soal kebutuhan khusus dan aturan setempat.

c. Bagi yang mempunyai jenazah, di tempat jenazah tersebut. 2. Amati karya: tidak boleh bekerja. 3. Amati lampah: tidak boleh bepergian, kecuali petilik desa dan prajuru dinas, serta mereka yang memperoleh izin dengan surat yang jelas. 4. Amati lelanguan: tidak boleh membuat suara keras, bersenang-senang/bermain, dan kegiatan sejenis.
(2) Pelanggar brata Nyepi dikenai sanksi menurut pararem, dilaksanakan oleh petilik desa dan Hansip. Denda dibagi tiga, masing-masing untuk desa, banjar, dan petilik/Hansip.
(3) Hari setelah Nyepi disebut Ngembak Geni, yang berarti berakhirnya yoga semadi, disertai saling memaafkan antar-krama desa/banjar sebagai tanda awal Tahun Saka.

V07.answer: On Nyepi, Canggu's customary village rules describe a day of four quiet observances for registered village members: no lighting fires, no working, no travelling, and no loud noise, parties or entertainment. They don't set out a separate list of rules for visitors, so this is local practice rather than a visitor obligation. As a guest, the respectful way to join in is to keep noise and music low, avoid open flames, and plan to stay close to your accommodation rather than moving around. The day is meant for calm and reflection, so the quiet mood is the main thing to respect.
V07.why_it_matters: Nyepi is a day of reflection and calm for the community, and keeping the quiet shows respect for your neighbours and the place you're visiting.

Plan to stay near your accommodation instead of travelling around.

V10.answer: Yes, please walk around it rather than over it. Canang sari is the small daily offering you'll see everywhere in Canggu — outside shops, homes, on the pavement, near shrines. Balinese Hindus place them as part of everyday worship, so they're not decoration or litter. If one is in your path, step around it where you can, and never kick, move or deliberately step on one. Offerings come in many different forms and meanings, so if you're unsure what you're looking at, just ask your host or a local guide — people are usually happy to explain.
V10.why_it_matters: These offerings are a daily act of prayer and gratitude for Balinese Hindus, so treating them with care is a simple sign of respect for the people whose neighbourhood you're sharing.

V11.answer: Galungan and Kuningan are two of the most important celebrations in Balinese Hindu religious life — a time of devotion and a celebration of dharma (goodness) prevailing over adharma (evil). They are genuinely religious occasions, not a festival put on for visitors, so you'll see real preparations around you: penjor (tall decorated bamboo poles), offerings, worship and processions, and often changes to business hours, traffic or access. If you come across a ceremony, watch quietly from a respectful distance, don't step into the worship, and just ask your host or a local guide what's appropriate. Villages don't all mark the days the same way.
V11.why_it_matters: For Balinese Hindus these days carry real spiritual weight, so joining in quietly and respectfully — rather than treating it as a show — is what people here appreciate.
recommended_actions: Ask your host or a local guide what is appropriate if you come across a ceremony
Watch from an appropriate place without disrupting worship
Expect and respect temporary changes to access, traffic or opening hours
Check a current calendar for the actual dates, since these shift

V13.answer: Yes to the helmet, and yes to carrying a proper licence. Bali's provincial rules, set out in a 2025 governor's circular for foreign visitors, ask anyone riding a scooter to wear a properly fastened helmet and to hold a valid national or international driving licence that's recognised here and right for the vehicle. Use a legally registered rental and check the bike is roadworthy before you set off. A short trip or a quiet road doesn't make any of this optional, and renting a scooter doesn't by itself give you the right to ride it.
V13.why_it_matters: Helmets, licences and registered rentals keep riders, passengers and pedestrians safer on Canggu's busy, narrow roads, and locals notice when visitors respect the same rules they do.
recommended_actions: Bring a valid national or international driving licence that covers a motorcycle and carry it with you
Wear a properly fastened helmet on every ride, however short
Rent from a legally registered rental business and check the scooter's condition first
Keep within the passenger limit and never ride after drinking

V16.why_it_matters: Canggu's streets are shared by visitors, residents, businesses and delivery riders, so moving respectfully keeps access open for everyone and lowers the chance of avoidable accidents.

V19.answer: No — please never throw rubbish into the river, the sea, or a roadside drain. Bali's provincial rules ban dumping waste into water and waterways, and Canggu's customary village rules (awig-awig / pararem) say the same for everyone in the village, guests included: no rubbish in drains, rivers, springs, the lake, the sea, roads or pavements. People here take water seriously — rivers and the sea carry offerings and are part of daily spiritual life, and blocked drains mean flooding in the wet season. Keeping your rubbish in a bag until you find a proper bin is the simple, respectful habit that locals appreciate.
V19.why_it_matters: Water is sacred to Balinese people and the rivers and sea are tied to temple life and offerings, so keeping them clean is a sign of respect as much as good hygiene.
recommended_actions: Keep your rubbish in a bag until you find a proper bin or your guesthouse's collection point.
Use the bins at your accommodation or a nearby café or warung rather than leaving waste on the street.
Ask your host where to put anything unusual, like batteries or broken glass.
Don't burn your rubbish or leave it in a drain, ditch or on the pavement.

V24.answer: The rules I can see apply across Bali, not specifically to Ubud, so treat them as the general temple etiquette wherever you go. Bali's provincial rules say nobody in a state of cuntaka or sebel (ritual impurity, often linked to recent bereavement or other sensitive circumstances) may enter a temple, and neither should anyone who isn't directly connected to a ceremony, a prayer gathering, or temple upkeep. So before stepping into a temple, check whether a ceremony is on and whether you're genuinely welcome as a visitor. Never damage or desecrate a temple, its sacred heirlooms (pratima) or religious symbols, and help keep the grounds clean by skipping single-use plastic.
V24.why_it_matters: Temples are the living heart of Balinese religious life, and keeping them pure and undamaged is how the community protects what is sacred to them.

Treat shrines, sacred objects and religious symbols with care and never touch or damage them
Avoid bringing single-use plastic into temple grounds

H01.answer: Yes, expect to. Canggu's customary village rules (awig-awig / pararem) record a monthly community contribution called sadana krama for people who live here but aren't registered village members, which is what you are as a newcomer. The same rules ask you to report to the local officials within about a week of arriving, with clear documents. Each banjar (the neighbourhood council) decides its own amount and how it's collected, so it's really a question for the banjar where you live rather than a set fee. Treat it as joining in the running of the neighbourhood, not a fine.
H01.why_it_matters: That contribution is how a banjar pays for shared life here, from ceremonies to helping neighbours, so joining in is part of being a good guest.

Ask which banjar area your accommodation sits in, so you pay the right one.
Check the sadana krama amount and payment routine directly with that banjar, or have your host introduce you.

H04.answer: Sebagai pemilik restoran di Canggu, Anda termasuk pihak yang wajib ikut mengelola sampah sendiri dengan baik, bukan hanya mengandalkan petugas. H04.why_it_matters: Bagi warga Canggu, kebersihan lingkungan adalah soal kebersamaan dan rasa hormat pada desa adat, dan usaha yang ikut menjaga akan lebih diterima oleh tetangga dan banjar (dewan lingkungan) setempat.

H05.answer: Drive on the left in Bali. Signal before you turn or change direction, keep your phone out of your hands while moving, and give pedestrians and cyclists space — the roads here are narrow and busy, so being predictable is what keeps everyone safe. Park only where it's permitted and never where you'd block traffic or a footpath. If you're riding a scooter, wear a properly fastened helmet and stay within the passenger limit; a short trip or quiet road doesn't make the basics optional.
H05.why_it_matters: On narrow, crowded Canggu roads, calm and predictable driving is a courtesy to neighbours and other road users as much as a rule.
recommended_actions: Drive on the left and signal before turning or changing direction
Park only where permitted, without blocking traffic or pedestrian paths
Wear a fastened helmet and respect passenger limits if riding a scooter
Pull over safely before checking your phone or navigation

H06.answer: No — better not. Bali's provincial rules are clear that you must never drive under the influence of alcohol or illegal drugs, and that includes a scooter. A short ride on a quiet road doesn't make it optional. If you're planning to drink, sort out a lift or a driver instead of riding. And whenever you do ride, wear a properly fastened helmet, keep to the passenger limit, and make sure your licence is valid for the vehicle and recognised here. Rental places hand over the keys, but the responsibility for riding safely stays with you.
H06.why_it_matters: Roads here are shared with families, workers and pedestrians, and police have made drink-driving, helmets and phone use real enforcement priorities — riding sober is how you look after the people around you as much as yourself.
recommended_actions: Skip the scooter entirely if you've been drinking and arrange a driver or ride instead
Wear a properly fastened helmet every time you ride, however short the trip
Carry a valid licence recognised in Indonesia and keep your vehicle documents with you
Check that your rental vehicle is properly registered and roadworthy before you set off

Ikuti aturan pakaian khusus yang dipasang di lokasi atau dijelaskan penyelenggara.

H08.answer: Tri Hita Karana is a Balinese way of thinking about a good life as three connected relationships: with the divine (parahyangan), between people (pawongan), and with nature (palemahan). You'll feel it here in the way temple shrines sit inside ordinary neighbourhoods, in how much people value getting along with their neighbours, and in everyday care for the environment. It's a broad framework rather than a fixed set of rules, and different villages and institutions emphasise it in their own ways, so it's best used as a lens for understanding what you see around you rather than a checklist.
H08.why_it_matters: Seeing these three relationships as connected helps explain why spiritual spaces, community harmony and care for the land are treated as one woven whole in Balinese life.
recommended_actions: Treat the three dimensions as a broad way of understanding what you see, not a complete explanation of every practice.
Ask local guides or community representatives how the concept is understood in your specific area of Canggu.
Notice how it shows up in daily life around you, from neighbourhood shrines to how people look after shared spaces.
